{{nihongo|'''Kohata Shrine'''|許波多神社|Kohata Jinja}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in {{ill|Uji|Q326956|qid=Q326956}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|Q120730|qid=Q120730}}. The shrine is dedicated to {{ill|Ame-no-oshihomimi|de|Amenooshihomimi|fa|آمه-نو-اوشیهومیمی|fr|Ame-no-oshihomimi|it|Ame-no-oshihomimi|ja|アメノオシホミミ|ko|아메노오시호미미|mni|ꯑꯃꯦ-ꯅꯣ-ꯑꯣꯁꯤꯍꯣꯃꯤꯃꯤ|ru|Амэноосихомими но Микото|th|อาเมะ โนะ โอชิโฮมิมิ|uk|Аменоосіхомімі но Мікото|zh|天忍穗耳尊|qid=Q462555|lt=Ame no Oshihomimi}}, the only {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286}} in Japan to enshrine this deity as its primary god. Listed in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]] as a {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|fr|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|simple|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|qid=Q9610964}} of [[Yamashiro Province]], it was formerly known as "Yanagi Daimyojin." In Uji City, there are two shrines bearing the name Kohata Shrine—one in {{ill|Kohata|Q11518385|qid=Q11518385}} and one in {{ill|Gokasho|Q135477391|qid=Q135477391}}—each with its own distinct history, and both formerly ranked as {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}}. The shrine is associated with legends of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|Q335181|qid=Q335181}} and {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|Q941979|qid=Q941979}} praying for victory in battle.

'''Kohata Shrine'' (Kohata Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|Q120730|qid=Q120730}}{{ill|Uji|Q326956|qid=Q326956}}. {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikiuchi Shrine}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|fr|Myōjin Taisha|ja|名神大社|simple|Myōjin Taisha|zh|名神大社|qid=Q9610964}}) This is Hiding Shrine of ``Kohata Shrine''. In Uji City, there are two shrines named Kōhata Shrine, {{ill|Kohata|Q11518385|qid=Q11518385}} and {{ill|Gokasho|Q135477391|qid=Q135477391}}. They are located in the district <ref> (However, according to ``Uji Promenade'' Volume 1, Higashi Uji Area Edition, p. 28, the former Kobata includes the current Gokasho)</ref>, and each has its own shrine history. The former {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|ko|사격 (신토)|zh|社格|qid=Q10444029}} are both {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}}. Formerly known as ``Yanagi Daimyojin''.In the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}, it is listed as Meishin Taisha.<ref>Kyoto Daijiten, Tankosha, 1984, p399</ref>. It is said that Prince Oama (later {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|Q335181|qid=Q335181}}) and {{ill|Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|Q941979|qid=Q941979}} prayed for victory in the war. p28</ref>, <ref> Kyoto Shimbun, "Encounter with the story: Horses and the tradition of bestowing luck: Kohata Shrine," March 18, 2001</ref>. The enshrined deity of both Kōhata Shrines is {{ill|Ame-no-oshihomimi|de|Amenooshihomimi|fa|آمه-نو-اوشیهومیمی|fr|Ame-no-oshihomimi|it|Ame-no-oshihomimi|ja|アメノオシホミミ|ko|아메노오시호미미|mni|ꯑꯃꯦ-ꯅꯣ-ꯑꯣꯁꯤꯍꯣꯃꯤꯃꯤ|ru|Амэноосихомими но Микото|th|อาเมะ โนะ โอชิโฮมิมิ|uk|Аменоосіхомімі но Мікото|zh|天忍穗耳尊|qid=Q462555|lt=Amaninhomi no Mikoto}} <ref>Historical Art Club, “History and Art,” “About Shikinai Taisha Kohata Shrine Sanza,” Shigeru Moriya, 1978, p42</ref>. Since Kōhata Shrine is the only Shikinai shrine that enshrines Tenninhomimi no Mikoto as the deity, it is written in {{ill|Shaku Nihongi|Q2710483|qid=Q2710483}} of the {{ill|Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205}} that ``The deity seated at Kōhata Shrine should be revered as the deity of the shrine, unlike the others.'' In the 12th year of {{ill|Eiroku|Q1143341|qid=Q1143341}} ({{ill|1569|Q6653|qid=Q6653}}), he received the highest rank of Shoichii {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|Q11591025|qid=Q11591025}}. After the war, neither of them joined {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}, but affiliated with {{ill|Jinja Honkyō|Q11590707|qid=Q11590707}}<ref>``Shinja Honkyo Calendar'' 2016 Edition</ref>.{{Citation required|During the Sengoku period, most of the shrine building was destroyed by fire during the war, and the old legend was also lost. |date=August 2017}}

In addition to Tennin Homimi no Mikoto, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|de|Ninigi|eo|Ninigi|es|Ninigi no Mikoto|fa|نینیگی-نو-میکوتو|fr|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|id|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|it|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|ja|ニニギ|ko|니니기|mni|ꯅꯤꯅꯤꯒꯤ-ꯅꯣ-ꯃꯤꯀꯣꯇꯣ|nl|Ninigi|no|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|pl|Ninigi|pt|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|ru|Ниниги но Микото|simple|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|sv|Ninigi|th|นินิงิ โนะ มิโกโตะ|tl|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|tr|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|uk|Нініґі но мікото|vi|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|zh|瓊瓊杵尊|qid=Q1056017|lt=Keirigi no Mikoto}}, the god of Japan Iwayohiko no Mikoto ({{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ar|الإمبراطور جينمو|arz|الامبراطور جينمو|as|জিম্মু|az|Cimmu|bcl|Emperador Jimmu|be|Імператар Дзіму|ca|Jinmu|cdo|Sìng-ū Tiĕng-huòng|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر جینمو|cs|Džimmu|de|Jimmu|el|Αυτοκράτορας Τζίμου|eo|Imperiestro Jinmu|es|Jinmu Tennō|et|Jimmu|eu|Jimmu enperadorea|fa|امپراتور جینمو|fi|Jinmu|fr|Jinmu|hak|Sṳ̀n-vú Thiên-fòng|he|ג'ימו, קיסר יפן|hi|सम्राट जिममु|hr|Jinmu|hu|Dzsinmu japán császár|id|Jimmu|it|Jinmu|ja|神武天皇|jv|Jimmu Tenno|ka|ძიმუ|ko|진무 천황|kw|Emperour Jimmu|la|Jimmu|lt|Imperatorius Džinmu|lv|Džimmu|mn|Эзэн Хаан Жиммү|mr|जिम्मू|ms|Maharaja Jimmu|my|ဂျင်းမူ ဧကရာဇ်|nl|Jimmu|no|Jimmu|pl|Jimmu|pt|Jimmu|ro|Împăratul Jimmu|ru|Император Дзимму|sh|Car Jimmu|simple|Emperor Jimmu|sl|Cesar Džinmu|sr|Џинму|sv|Jimmu|th|จักรพรรดิจิมมุ|tl|Emperador Jimmu|tr|Jimmu|uk|Імператор Дзімму|uz|Jimmu|vi|Thiên hoàng Jimmu|war|Emperador Jimmu|wuu|神武天皇|zh|神武天皇|zh_classical|神武天皇|zh_min_nan|Sîn-bú Thian-hông|zh_yue|神武天皇|qid=Q200188}}) is enshrined here.

According to the shrine biography, in the first year of {{ill|Taika (era)|Q1077930|qid=Q1077930}} ({{ill|645|Q31040|qid=Q31040}}), {{ill|Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro|Q3488899|qid=Q3488899}} enshrined Emperor Kotoku. It is said that |Q317980}} ordered {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|Q433995|qid=Q433995|lt=Nakatomi Kamatari}} to build a temple to enshrine the imperial ancestors in Yanagiyama, Kuniujigunkohata, Udo District, Yamashiro Province. Because the shrine was located on the land of Yanagiyama, it later came to be called ``Yanagi Daimyojin,'' and its official name was ``Yanagi Shrine'' until the Edo period. During the Meiji period, {{ill|Imperial Japanese Army|Q276535|qid=Q276535|lt=Army}} Uji Gunpowder Factory (currently The entire shrine grounds were taken over as government land for the construction of the {{ill|Japan Ground Self-Defense Force|Q889751|qid=Q889751}}{{ill|JGSDF Camp Uji|Q11449523|qid=Q11449523}}), and our company was {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=transferred}} to its current location, which was {{ill|Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117}}, and at that time the company name was changed to the former Kōhata Shrine.A {{ill|Idols in Shinto|Q11588751|qid=Q11588751}} of a pair of men and women ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Bazu Tenno}} and {{ill|Benzaiten|qid=Q818468|lt=Benzaiten}}), said to have been made in the late Heian period, is said to have been enshrined in the attached temple. The main shrine enshrines a statue of Tenninhomi no Mikoto, said to have been created during the Kamakura period.

It is believed that in the past, horse racing rituals were held on the Baba-michi road that runs from the main shrine building to the two towns of East and West, and is said to be the ``Shrine that originated {{ill|Horse racing|Q187916|qid=Q187916}}.'' The {{ill|Stirrup|Q191657|qid=Q191657}} (stirrup) from the Heian period, which remains as a shrine treasure, is designated as {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622}}. In addition, there is a statue of Bazu Tenno, so it is known as a ``horse shrine'' and is worshiped by horse racing fans and people involved in horse racing.

== Kohata Shrine before relocation ==
{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Relocation}}The previous Kōhata Shrine was located in Yanagiyama (near present-day Obaku Park in Uji City), where it was founded, and the road extending west from there was the approach to Kōhata Shrine. Proceeding west along the road from Obaku Park and beyond the JR and Keihan railroad crossings, there used to be a shrine's Ichinotorii gate, but during the Meiji period, the upper part of the torii gate was removed, and now only the lower part, the Kutsuishi, remains. The remaining stone is also called the ``Kyoto University Moai,'' and is a reminder of the former Kōhata Shrine that was enshrined in Yanagiyama. Additionally, in front of the gymnasium in Obaku Park, where the main shrine is said to have been located before its relocation, the base of the main shrine has now been restored and willows have been planted.

According to the company biography, in the first year of {{ill|Taika (era)|Q1077930|qid=Q1077930}} ({{ill|645|Q31040|qid=Q31040}}), {{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|Q235296|qid=Q235296|lt=Emperor Kogyoku}} was a dream. It is said that he received a message saying, ``Since I am Tenjin, there will be a tomb for the god in the lower soil, and I will enshrine the spirits there.'' He ordered {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|Q433995|qid=Q433995|lt=Nakatomi Kamatari}} to build a shrine at Kobata-no-sho. When Prince Oama headed from Otsunomiya to Yoshino ahead of the {{ill|Jinshin War|bg|Войната Джиншин|ca|Guerra Jinshin|es|Guerra Jinshin|fa|شورش جینشین|fr|Guerre de Jinshin|id|Pertempuran Jinshin|it|Guerra jinshin|ja|壬申の乱|ko|진신의 난|pl|Zamieszki roku Jinshin|pt|Guerra Jinshin|ru|Смута года Дзинсин|sh|Džinšinski rat|simple|Jinshin War|sl|Džinšinska vojna|su|Perang Jinshin|th|สงครามจินชิน|tr|Jinshin Savaşı|uk|Смута Дзінсін|vi|Chiến tranh Jinshin|zh|壬申之亂|qid=Q2378252}}, he placed a willow branch at the head of the shrine and prayed for victory, saying, ``If I ascend to the throne, this willow will sprout.'' It is said that when Prince Oama ascended the throne, a willow branch sprouted, and the Emperor gave him the name ``Yanagi Daimyojin'' and donated the shrine's territory in praise of his miraculous powers.

It is said to have been enshrined at its current location from Yanagiyama during the Oho era (1161-1163) <ref>``Japan Historical Place Names Daikei Volume 26 Place Names of Kyoto Prefecture'' Heibonsha, 1981, p227</ref>.1908 (ref) “Uji City History 3: Early Modern History and Landscape”, 1975, p457 Table 43. In addition, the history of the shrine states, ``Additional note: In January 1907, Tanaka Shrine was enshrined and continued to this day.'' Since Tanaka Shrine in the former Kawara Village was enshrined in </ref>, the company's enshrined deities {{ill|Amaterasu|abstract|Q455602|ar|أماتيراسو|ary|أماطيراسو|az|Amaterasu|bcl|Amaterasu|be|Аматэрасу|be_x_old|Аматэрасу|bew|Amatérasu|bg|Аматерасу|ca|Amaterasu|cs|Amaterasu|da|Amaterasu|de|Amaterasu|el|Αματεράσου|eo|Amaterasu|es|Amaterasu|et|Amaterasu|eu|Amaterasu|fa|آماتراسو|fi|Amaterasu|fr|Amaterasu|gl|Amaterasu|he|אמטראסו|hi|अमातेरसु|hr|Amaterasu|hu|Amateraszu Ómikami|hy|Ամատերասու Օմիկամի|id|Amaterasu|it|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|jv|Amaterasu|ka|ამატერასუ|ko|아마테라스 오미카미|la|Amaterasu|lb|Amaterasu|lt|Amaterasu|lv|Amaterasu|min|Amaterasu|ml|അമതേരസു|mni|ꯑꯃꯇꯦꯔꯁꯨ ꯑꯣꯃꯤꯀꯃꯤ|ms|Amaterasu|nl|Amaterasu|nn|Amaterasu|no|Amaterasu|or|ଆମାତେରାଶୁ|pa|ਆਮਾਤੇਰਸ|pl|Amaterasu|pt|Amaterasu|ro|Amaterasu|rsk|Аматерасу|ru|Аматэрасу|sco|Amaterasu|sh|Amaterasu|simple|Amaterasu Ōmikami|sk|Amaterasu Ómikami|sl|Amaterasu|sr|Аматерасу|su|Amaterasu|sv|Amaterasu|ta|அமதெரசு|th|อามาเตราซุ|tl|Amaterasu|tok|jan sewi suli Amatelasu|tr|Amaterasu|uk|Аматерасу|uz|Amaterasu|vi|Amaterasu|wuu|天照大神|zh|天照大神|zh_min_nan|Amaterasu|zh_yue|天照大神|qid=Q455602|lt=Amaterasu Omikami}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amatsu Hikone-no-Mikoto}} are also enshrined there.

Within the precincts, there is Tomb No. 36 of {{ill|Uji Mausolea|Q38277767|qid=Q38277767}} called ``Foxzuka,'' which is said to be the tomb of {{ill|Fujiwara no Mototsune|Q1397196|qid=Q1397196}}.
